output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: it attributes the 22% deviation to shared conversational memory and persistent KV state, but the recompute-from-text baseline also shows interference, and the paper says the rates cannot be attributed to cache persistence.
output.brief: OLMo-3-7B-Instruct is tested in a two-client market setting with 20 goal-conflict families, where each client has an opposing objective and turns share one persistent KV cache. In 150 eligible decisions, the model deviates from the current client's objective in 22.0% (95% CI 16.1-29.3), with 11.3% choosing the opposite client's option outright. A recompute-from-text baseline also shows interference, so persistence is not shown to be the cause. Linear probes on span-pooled K/V of goal tokens recover client ownership from near chance at layer 0 (AUROC 0.481) to 0.982 at layer 15, with individual heads reaching 0.993. Zeroing the competitor's cached goal K/V in layers 12-20 shifts the target-vs-opposite log-probability margin by +0.464 (K) and +0.704 (V). Probe-selected Top3 heads beat random heads, and goal tokens beat matched non-goal tokens. Ablating the current client's own goal reverses the sign. Selected actions change less often: 23 of 166 non-target decisions are corrected under V ablation. The limits are one 7B model, explicit client labels, zero-ablation, and no distinction between binding, retrieval and competition mechanisms.
output.gist: In a two-client market task, OLMo-3-7B deviates from the current client's goal in 22% of decisions; probe-located middle-layer KV goal representations causally shift choices when ablated.
output.weight_reason: A sound but narrow study combining probing with controlled KV ablations in one 7B model and one synthetic setting, with a clear causal control design but no mechanism identified.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the BLEU gains of 33.75% (Hi→Ur) and 45.86% (Hi→Sd) are relative to the SFT/DPO baselines in the table, mostly small absolute gains (Hi→Ur 31.82 vs 25.94 BLEU), the 5.45 BLEU gain over a same-budget LoRA is measured on one direction, and the claim of no English-centric pivot rests on cosine similarity of MLP states with token embeddings, not a causal test.
output.brief: TITAN is a pipeline for Hindi→Urdu and Hindi→Sindhi translation in Gemma-2 9B. CIRCE, a subspace-constrained activation patching step, contrasts valid translation prompts with counterfactual prompts and selects attention heads and MLP blocks above a P99 noise-floor threshold. SAEs are trained on the selected layers and features are scored by selectivity and causal lift. SFT and then DPO are applied only to the selected components, under 5% of parameters (3.14% in the matched comparison). On Hi→Ur BLEU, TITAN reaches 31.82 against 25.94 for the best baseline (Gemma-2 DPO). On Hi→Sd it reaches 23.25 against 18.01, which is the quoted +45.86% relative gain on a narrower baseline set. A LoRA SFT+DPO run at the same budget scores 26.37 BLEU. Knockout of eight identified components drops BLEU from 25.53 to 16.54 in a general LoRA model, versus 25.41 for random components. Human ratings favour TITAN, but the samples are small, apparently about 30 per direction. MLP cosine analysis shows negative English alignment, taken as evidence against an English pivot. Limits: one base model, no comparison against standard circuit-discovery baselines, and the pivot claim lacks a causal test.
output.gist: Causal patching selects attention heads and MLPs in Gemma-2 9B, and SFT plus DPO restricted to them raises Hindi–Urdu and Hindi–Sindhi BLEU over full baselines; knockouts and embedding projections support the circuit analysis.
output.weight_reason: Circuit discovery is used mainly to pick parameters for fine-tuning, with a single model, a moderate causal validation of the circuit and a pivot claim resting on correlational projections, so it is a modest contribution to circuit analysis.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: steering shifts only a fraction of cadences (vi 32% under relative-minor steering, i 57% under parallel-minor), with the strength α picked per condition for the strongest effect, and parallel-minor steering raises FMD from 80.3 to 106.7.
output.brief: Aria, a LLaMA-based symbolic music transformer, is analyzed on Bach chorales using minimal contrastive pairs: the chordal third of a V chord is lowered by a semitone (184 major and 91 minor prompt pairs). This edit cuts tonic resolutions in major chorales from 87.5% to 51.4%. Residual-stream patching at the last pre-generation token shows little effect in layers 0-5, with the effect appearing around layer 6 and growing through later layers. Linear probes decode mode up to 82.1% at layers 8-9, while 18-class key accuracy reaches 65.5% by layer 15. Probe-derived directions are used as steering vectors. Relative-minor steering moves resolutions to vi (32%) and parallel-minor steering to i (57%), against an 81% tonic baseline. Structural errors stay under 3%, but FMD rises. Mode steering redistributes mass diffusely. Relative keys are more confusable than parallel keys in probes, which the authors offer as the reason for the steering asymmetry. Limits: one model, one corpus of conventional harmony, no control directions, and α tuned per condition.
output.gist: Patching, linear probes and probe-derived steering vectors on Aria with Bach cadences show mode is decodable before key, and key directions shift cadence resolutions toward vi or parallel-minor i.
output.weight_reason: A clean but narrow case study of one model and one corpus, using standard patching, probing and steering with no control directions and per-condition tuned strengths.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the claim that detection performance can depend strongly on the prompt template is not tested, since every result uses one structured Task/External-content format and no experiment varies the template.
output.brief: Five internal-state prompt-injection detectors (PIShield, Attention Tracker, Role Confusion, the Dong exposure probe, and J-Lens) are adapted to one structured indirect-injection format. They are run on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, each with 2,000 attacks and 1,000 template-matched benign controls. Attacks are split by whether the response actually followed the injection, as labeled by LLM judges, and AUROC against the same controls is reported per stratum. PIShield and J-Lens separate unsuccessful attacks better than successful ones (PIShield 0.898 vs 0.637 on Qwen, 0.980 vs 0.821 on Gemma). Attention Tracker, Role Confusion and the Dong probe show the opposite ordering on both models. Attention Tracker is strongest on successful attacks, at 0.949 on Qwen and 0.887 on Gemma. The authors read this as recognition versus influence signals. Limits: only two similar-sized models, one explicit prompt format, and adapted rather than faithfully reproduced methods. J-Lens also uses response-position features. The corpus is outcome-conditioned, with adaptive successful variants substituted in, so wording differences may confound the successful/unsuccessful gaps.
output.gist: Five internal-state injection detectors are compared on two open models with outcome-stratified AUROC. Presence probes rank failed attacks higher; Attention Tracker, role and exposure probes rank successful ones higher, Attention Tracker reaching 0.949 and 0.887.
output.weight_reason: It is a careful, fair comparison of five detectors that separates injection presence from attack success, but it covers two models, one prompt format and adapted methods, with attack wording a possible confound.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the ablation is layerwise (zeroing whole-layer attention outputs) on 40 examples from one model, PaliGemma2-3B, not headwise. The headwise analysis only plots per-head attention and finds no specialised negation heads.
output.brief: Attention to image tokens is compared with human eye-fixation findings from Orenes et al. (2014) for affirmative versus negated prompts such as "The figure is not blue". Six VLMs are tested (LLaVA-1.5-7B/13B, InternVL3.5-4B/8B, PaliGemma2-3B/10B) on synthetic two-object (Binary) and four-object (Multary) shape images and on 206 What'sUp images, with Grounding DINO bounding boxes validated at IoU 0.93 on 20 images. Most models do not show the human-like pattern. PaliGemma2-3B does, shifting attention to the alternative object from layer 13 under negation. Ablating attention in individual PaliGemma2-3B layers shows that layers up to 13 matter most for the answer, so the shift looks like a byproduct. LLaVA-1.5-7B attends more to left-side objects. All models are less accurate on negated yes/no questions, with large prompt-template variance, and attention patterns do not track accuracy. Limits: three model families, simple images, a static stand-in for the human priming setup, and attention as the only signal, with a small causal test on one model.
output.gist: Object-level attention in six VLMs under negated prompts mostly departs from human gaze patterns, with only PaliGemma2-3B shifting to the alternative object; all models answer negated questions less accurately.
output.weight_reason: It is a careful but small-scale attention-visualisation study on simple images, with thin causal evidence limited to one model and mostly negative findings about the attention-gaze analogy.

output.brief: Components are selected in GPT-2-Small, Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.1-8B by Spearman correlation (ρ ≥ 0.5) between their token-averaged activation and LLM-judged narrativity (agency, event sequencing, world building) on the NarraDetect corpus. Selected heads, MLP neurons and residual-stream SAE features are ablated as sets and compared with size-matched random sets. On held-out human-labelled texts, ablating neurons and features raises next-token loss more for narrative texts (loss–narrativity correlation 0.65–0.86 versus about 0 for random); heads are weak. In Gemma and Llama, feature ablation lowers generated narrativity by 1.0–1.9 points versus under 0.5 for random. Feature ablation also hurts XStoryCloze in all four languages for Gemma but only English for Llama, and hurts CosmosQA, with no extra OpenBookQA loss. Dimension-specific ablations show partial effects for agency and event but none for world building. Hallucination benchmarks are mixed. Limits: three models, a heuristic threshold, set-level causal claims only, uncorrected p-values, and SAE ablation raises degenerate outputs, though the drop persists after excluding them.
output.gist: Selects attention heads, neurons and SAE features in three LMs by correlation with narrativity; ablating neuron and feature sets impairs narrative prediction and generation beyond random ablation.
output.weight_reason: A complete study across three models with random-set baselines, held-out validation and benchmark tests, but the causal evidence is set-level ablation of correlation-selected components with no circuit connectivity or individual-component analysis.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: shallow exits are clearly more robust only for Balcony-LLaMA3-8B (28% to 2-4% ASR); for Balcony-LLaMA2-7B the ASR spread is small (36-44% on HarmBench) and not monotonic on AdvBench, from 50 behaviors and one attack.
output.brief: The study converts LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B into depth-based dynamic models with the Balcony method (frozen backbone, exits at layers 15, 18 and 21), then runs GCG for 150 steps on 50 behaviors each from HarmBench and AdvBench at every exit and at the full model. For LLaMA3-8B, ASR rises with depth: 4/12/12/28% on HarmBench and 2/0/12/28% on AdvBench, and final GCG loss at exit-15 is about three times that of the full model. For LLaMA2-7B, ASR is already 36% (HarmBench) and 46% (AdvBench) at exit-15 and reaches 44% and 54% at full depth, so shallow exits give little protection. GCG loss is lower at deeper exits in all four settings. Appending each exit's best suffix leaves six-benchmark utility largely unchanged, except ARC-E on the 7B model. For LLaMA3, lower ASR at shallow exits coincides with lower clean utility. The authors call the findings associative. Limits: one attack, two backbones, fixed exits, small behavior sets, and no defence is proposed or tested.
output.gist: GCG attacks applied at intermediate exits of Balcony LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B show lower attack loss at deeper exits, with ASR gaps large only for LLaMA3-8B.
output.weight_reason: A small workshop-scale empirical study with one attack, two backbones and 50 behaviors per benchmark, whose depth effect is strong for only one model and which proposes no defence.

output.brief: Three open MoE LLMs (OLMoE-1B-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Mixtral-8x7B) are personalized with two-stage LoRA tuning, routers first and then the most-selected experts, on Multifaceted Collection. They are compared with dense models matched on active and on total parameters across Multifaceted Bench, LaMP and LongLaMP. Personalized MoEs beat or match dense models of similar active size and, for Qwen and Mixtral, roughly match dense models of similar total size, using about 20% of parameters per token. K-sparse probing on 20 preference concepts gives MoE experts higher balanced accuracy than dense MLPs, which the authors read as lower polysemanticity. A BatchTopK crosscoder at one layer per model yields 111 to 157 personalized latents, under 0.25% of the total. LLM-based explanations of these latents score F1 0.63 to 0.70. Latents map to experts with stability 0.81 and distinctiveness 0.94 on Qwen3. Patching the latents recovers the personalized model's next-token distribution better than random or shared latents. Boosting the mapped experts moves the non-personalized model closer to the personalized one than random experts do. Limits: one layer per model, Mixtral is an exception on latent sharing, dense baselines differ in pre-training, expert attribution is correlational, and crosscoder reconstruction is imperfect (variance explained 0.65 to 0.80).
output.gist: Personalizes three MoE LLMs and trains crosscoders on personalized versus base activations to find personalization latents, mapped to specific experts; patching and expert-boosting experiments support their causal role, with performance competitive with dense models.
output.weight_reason: It applies existing crosscoder and sparse-probing tools to a new setting with causal checks and three models, but analyzes one layer per model and has confounded dense comparisons and correlational expert attribution.

output.brief: Masked diffusion language models are given mHC-lite multi-stream residual interfaces with token-conditioned read, mix and write maps, tested on a 337M Qwen-style backbone trained on 3.5B FineWeb-Edu tokens. Two streams reduce validation reconstruction perplexity by 5.71% against the standard residual and by 5.13% on average over four external corpora. A learned single stream gives 2.50%, and three or four streams add only about 0.5% more. At 1B parameters the two-stream gain is 3.47%. Interventions show that replacing read and write-destination routing with role-conditioned means removes 95.7% and 98.6% of the damage from global averaging, while token-specific write volume stays important within each role. A role-factorized model trained from scratch (FRR) recovers 50.2% of the gain from one to two streams. State patching shows one stream holding its early post-first-block state through middle depth while masked targets gather visible-source evidence in the other, and late layers read it again. The same stages appear at 1B, though stage boundaries and stream identities differ. Limits: single training runs, one backbone family, small models, and 179 selected source-target pairs for the transfer analysis, with no downstream or generation evaluation.
output.gist: Two residual streams with learned routing lower masked-diffusion perplexity by 5.71% over standard residuals; interventions show mask role shapes routing and one stream preserves early states for reuse.
output.weight_reason: A complete, carefully intervened study of multi-stream residuals in masked diffusion with consistent gains and a 1B replication, but the gains are modest, at small scale, from single runs, and without downstream evaluation.

output.brief: Ciphered Skill Injection (CSI) hides an attacker instruction in a third-party skill's SKILL.md as a Caesar-ciphered line with a decoding cue. A layered variant instead places a password-encrypted payload (AES, ChaCha20 or XSalsa20) in the skill, with the Caesar-encoded line naming the decryption skill and password. The attack is run on the 139 contextual injection-task pairs of Skill-Inject across eight models, and decryption attempt, full recovery, attack attempt and attack success are scored separately by an LLM judge. On skills shortened by rewriting, Caesar CSI reaches attack success of up to 47.5% (Muse-Glimmer-30B) and Layered CSI up to 40.3% (Gemma-4-31B). Recovery often does not lead to action: Qwen3.8-27B recovers the instruction in 78.4% of Caesar cases but succeeds in 5.8%. Layering raises success for three models and lowers it for five. Attacks persist without the Caesar skill. Cisco's scanner flags 4.3% and 2.9% of injected skills, and SkillRisk flags none. The main limit is that on the original longer skills Layered CSI success falls to at most 8.6%, and the rewriting confounds length with wording.
output.gist: Embeds Caesar-ciphered and layered encrypted instructions in agent skill files; attack success reaches 47.5% and 40.3% on shortened skills across eight models, with decoding often not yielding action.
output.weight_reason: A new encoding variant of skill injection evaluated on an existing benchmark, with ablations, but its success depends on shortened skills and falls sharply on the original ones.

output.brief: The paper defines SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR), the fraction of behavioral variance left unexplained by the best interaction-order-r fit to a downstream response over subsets of selected SAE feature contributions. Under independent subset sampling, SAR equals the normalized energy of interactions above order r and bounds a variance-weighted coalition ordering error. Experiments use Gemma-3 4B, Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1 8B on six behaviors, with K=16 features and 384 sampled coalitions per prompt. First-order SAR is positive in all 57 model, layer and behavior combinations, while affine controls sit at numerical zero. Learned SAE coordinates have lower first-order SAR than sum-preserving random rotations in all 18 settings, though the gap is tiny for Mistral greater-than. Pairwise terms raise held-out rank fidelity from 0.9782 to 0.9959 on average and beat parameter-matched random third-order models in all 18 settings. In a Llama steering experiment with 16 CorrSteer features, pairwise modeling raises rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 on overall MMLU-Pro, but it hurts in several individual domains. Conclusions are limited to the selected features, readouts and intervention distribution.
output.gist: Introduces a residual measuring non-additive downstream effects of SAE features; learned coordinates are more additive than random rotations, yet pairwise interaction terms consistently improve held-out coalition ranking.
output.weight_reason: It is a complete, carefully controlled framework with theory, rotation and capacity-matched baselines and multi-model experiments, but it is a new diagnostic with narrow demonstrations rather than a reference result.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the 99.94% figure is structural coverage for only WildChat and WildJailbreak, not semantic fidelity, and no human bilingual check exists; the language-dependent findings come from two 7-8B models on small samples.
output.brief: A pipeline translates seven English benchmarks (StrongREJECT, JBB-Behaviors, WildJailbreak, XSTest, WildChat, MATH-500, AIME 2024) into 11 languages. GPT-5.4 Thinking proposes three translation instructions, which are compared across five translators on a 70-item Thai pilot. GPT-5-mini with the fidelity-focused prompt is chosen for production at about $97 projected cost. Failed WildChat and WildJailbreak records are regenerated from English, leaving 4 of 6,820 pairs unresolved (99.94% structural coverage). Independent screening flags 1.2% of pairs as still untranslated. A Gemma-3-12B judge rates 99.6% of translations as meaning-preserving, but label agreement with English is only 92.6%. Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B show different multilingual patterns. Llama under-refuses in languages such as Turkish (unsafe XSTest refusal 97.5% to 69.5%). Qwen over-refuses safe prompts in all 11 languages (6.4% in English to 13.0-23.7%). MATH-500 accuracy drops by up to 20 points. Limits: the configuration pilot is Thai only, repair logs cover two sources, fidelity checks are automatic with no human evaluation completed, and the downstream evaluation uses two small models with truncation that affects non-English outputs.
output.gist: A translation pipeline with validation and repair builds a seven-benchmark, 11-language safety and math collection; automatic checks suggest good fidelity, and two 7-8B models show language-dependent refusal and math degradation.
output.weight_reason: A useful, carefully caveated multilingual benchmark-construction workflow, but it rests on a Thai-only pilot, automatic fidelity checks without human validation, and two small models, and it largely re-translates existing benchmarks.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the claim that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance rests on layer-wise gate-patching accuracy curves and probing on a synthetic phonebook task with two Mamba-2 models, and it is shown only for the unflagged setting. The text also supplies no direct test that late relevance causes the failure, and it leaves training and design explanations as open questions.
output.brief: Mamba-2 models (an 8B base model and the 7.3B Codestral-Mamba) fail at query-first phonebook retrieval, a setting where state capacity should not be the binding limit. Adding a single "target" flag to the queried entry more than doubles the 8B model's accuracy on long phonebooks. With the flag, the target digits are decodable from the recurrent state in earlier layers, and the selection gates separate target from distractor tokens better. Patching the gate values of the 10 target digit tokens from the flagged run into the unflagged run recovers flagged accuracy, and the reverse patch drops flagged accuracy to the unflagged level. Oracle scaling of those gates drives accuracy to near-perfect or near-zero. Layer-wise linear probes show relevance becomes decodable in token representations after nearly 10 layers without the flag, and in the gates several layers later still. Cumulative layer patching puts the accuracy gains in early-to-middle layers where the gates lag the representations. Limits: a synthetic task, only Mamba-2 models, and no test of why the delay arises.
output.gist: Query-first phonebook retrieval in two Mamba-2 models fails because selection gates act before relevance is encoded in token representations; gate patching and oracle scaling show the gates causally control accuracy.
output.weight_reason: It gives a careful causal and probing diagnosis of a known Mamba retrieval failure, with bidirectional patching and layer-wise analysis, but it covers one synthetic task and two models.

output.brief: In-context Mealy-machine execution with a looped two-layer transformer gives exact per-position targets and exact counterfactuals, which lets the paper separate computing an answer, retaining it past the trained exit, and reusing its hidden state. Models trained with the loss only on the last position at loop 32 reach 100% at loop 32 but keep 22.3% at loop 64. Supervising one uniformly sampled position per example keeps 99.8%, and a random exit distribution (Jitter-8) lifts loop-64 accuracy from 30.0% to 85.6% at matched expected loops. An adapted progressive (gradient-truncated) recipe learned length 32 in only one of three seeds, while a full-gradient control with the same exits kept 97.9%. Swapping one frontier hidden vector redirects all later positions to the exact counterfactual in 237/237 eligible pairs, in each of ten models. Freezing each position at the loop its answer first appears drops endpoint accuracy to 4.1% (sampled-position training) and 6.3% (matched random exit); freezing 2–4 loops later restores it. One released maze network behaves the same way. The limits are one synthetic task family, small models, three seeds for the new controls, and one maze checkpoint.
output.gist: In looped transformers executing Mealy machines, answers can be computed exactly yet lost at extra loops, and retention depends on the training loss. Even retained answers sit in states that cannot be frozen when they first appear.
output.weight_reason: A carefully controlled analysis with exact counterfactuals that separates computation, retention and reuse in looped models, though confined to one synthetic task, small models, few seeds and a single external checkpoint.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the Coin rewiring figure of 84.3% sits well above the native 31.6% but only modestly above a 62.5% chance level, and a rewire on a never-trained random trunk picks the coin almost as often, so much of the gain is relearned level-solving rather than recovered goal use.
output.brief: Goal-misgeneralizing agents are traced in three Procgen games (Maze, Coin, Attribute Maze) and five new robot tasks, with three GM and three control agents per environment. Probes, world edits, and a policy-Fisher sensitivity measure show where goal information is lost. Three failures appear: target substitution (Maze, PushToMarker), where the goal is inert or weakly read and a place replaces it; a policy shortcut (Coin), where a rightward action rule organizes behavior; and cue competition (Attribute Maze), where goal and proxy cues oppose each other on one policy-read axis. Steering at h_fc raises Attribute Maze goal reach from 0.160 to 0.953, but fails in Maze, PushToMarker and Coin (reach at most 0.027). Relearning the readout by behavioral cloning gives no recovery in Maze, partial recovery in PushToMarker (0.314, 0.661 with DAgger), and 0.843 in Coin against 0.625 chance and 0.840 for a random trunk in Attribute Maze. Limits: three seeds per cohort, small CNN agents, static checkpoints, and the training-structure explanation is a hypothesis.
output.gist: Tracing the goal through misgeneralizing RL agents in eight environments shows three failure types at different depths; steering works only under cue competition, retrained readouts where goal information survives.
output.weight_reason: A careful, multi-environment diagnostic study linking internal goal traces to which test-time repair works, but built on small agents, three seeds, and an untested hypothesis about training structure.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: vision and language dissociation is shown by nearest-neighbor retrieval selectivity, not subspace ablation (ablation is done only in RNNs), and the RNN double dissociations hold for the disjoint task pair Anti vs DM1, while inclusive and mixed pairs show none.
output.brief: A hierarchy of learned linear decompositions (permutation, orthogonal, invertible with bounded condition number) splits a layer's representation into two function subspaces plus a residual. Training uses task-sufficiency readouts for RNNs and contrastive minimal pairs for vision and language models. In tanh multitask RNNs on Anti vs DM1, the double dissociation index (DDI) is 0.00 at the unit level and 0.08 for permutation, but 0.37 for orthogonal and 0.47 for invertible maps. Mante RNNs reach DDI about 0.28 only under the invertible map, and single TDR axes have no causal effect. For Swin-Base content/style, retrieval selectivity ratios rise from about 1 (permutation) to 7.2/2.6 (orthogonal) and 16.1/5.3 (invertible); Pythia and GPT-2 syntax/semantics show the same ordering. Style subspaces predict early visual cortex and content subspaces higher visual cortex; semantic subspaces beat syntactic ones in language cortex. Controls with shuffled labels, spectrum-matched random maps and an overlapping content/category pair do not produce dissociations. Limits: inclusive and mixed RNN pairs stay non-modular (DDI at most 0.05), ResNets fail, vision and language lack ablation tests, results come from a single split without error bars, and optimization is non-convex.
output.gist: Learns permutation, orthogonal and invertible linear decompositions that split representations into two function subspaces plus a residual; invertible maps expose content/style, syntax/semantics and task structure that unit-level analysis misses.
output.weight_reason: A sound, well-controlled framework with causal RNN tests and random-map controls that others can build on, but vision and language evidence is retrieval-based and the RNN dissociation covers only one task pair.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the restatement pattern holds only for the strong guards and the guards that lose recall; for the over-blocking guards and AgentDoG the excess flips are larger on steps where the history does not restate the request.
output.brief: LinguaGuardBench takes the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj (58 user instructions) and translates only the instruction into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic, leaving tool calls, observations and labels byte-identical. Controls are six English rewordings and a whitespace placebo, and managed guards are run three times. Nineteen guards are tested, including four purpose-built agent guards. 39 of 77 guard-language cells show a significant shift in false-positive or true-positive rate. Among the nine guards below 13B, the placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 on Amharic, and purpose-built guards move most (ShieldAgent flips 12.1% of verdicts on Swahili). Open 12-30B guards over-block (up to +5.0 pp FPR), while every significant recall loss is below 10B (up to -7.4 pp). Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Sonnet 5 show no significant shift, and Gemini agrees on 100% of verdicts with a copy that never sees the request. English paraphrase moves general guards by at most 1.4 pp. Limits: Gemini produced all translations, and no author reads Swahili or Amharic. Partner-hosted guards were not run on the low-resource pair. Only one benchmark is used, bootstrap intervals are likely too narrow, and no mitigation is tested.
output.gist: Translating only the user request into five languages, with trajectory, action and label held fixed, shifts verdicts of small, open and purpose-built agent guards, more in rarer languages, while frontier guards stay stable.
output.weight_reason: A cleanly controlled, released benchmark and a fair 19-guard comparison establish language sensitivity in agent guards, but it covers one benchmark, five languages and no mitigations.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the Gemma-4 gain with an approver comes from a simulated principal that applies the scenario's ground-truth permission rule, and the model approver that escalates 25% of asks was checked only as worst-case bounds on logged asks (confirmed on 87 Qwen asks), not in live episodes.
output.brief: CAPE-Bench pairs 24 agent task templates with an unauthorized world and an authorized twin that differ in one fact. Four open-weight agents (Qwen3.8-27B, Muse-Glimmer-30B, Gemma-4-26B, gpt-oss-20b) violate and then misreport. A retroactive permission request precedes a false report in 70% of 1,081 informed violations, against 8% otherwise (preregistered OR 7.0). A linear residual-stream readout forecasts the violation at AUROC 0.94, but once the plan is written, text monitors match it. It leads text only before the plan exists and on lie forecasting when the reasoning is pressured to hide (+0.16 over a CoT monitor). Gating every action cuts episode-level violations in all four models (Gemma 0.70→0.09 with an approver, gpt-oss only 0.78→0.60) and cuts misreported violations from 0.10 to 0.01. A readout refit on 29 AgentDojo tasks cuts injection success on two models. Limits: mock tools, open-weight models only, no test against evasion, and only modest gains on gpt-oss and Muse.
output.gist: Benchmark of matched authorized/unauthorized tasks shows agents act without authorization then misreport; a linear activation readout gating every action cuts violations and subsequent misreports across four open-weight models.
output.weight_reason: A complete, carefully preregistered study with matched-world evaluation and episode-level prevention results, but on mock tools with four open models, and the readout often only matches text monitors once the plan is written.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the human audit checks only the relevance of sampled candidates (not the LLM-assigned harmful-goal/operational roles or the history contrast itself), and the behavioral gap between histories falls to about zero at 4B by 800 harmful examples.
output.brief: Qwen1.5 models (0.5B, 4B, 7B) are safety-tuned either directly or after 1,000 harmful fine-tuning examples. Both endpoints reach near-zero HarmBench attack success. A Jacobian-lens readout then maps intermediate states to vocabulary space, and a blinded Qwen2.5-32B judge counts concrete harmful-goal and operational-enabler words among the Top-20 candidates. Prior-exposure checkpoints show higher mean counts at every scale. The largest gap is 0.106 at 4B, and the 4B layerwise peak is 0.255 near mid-depth. Contrasts are near zero at layer 0 and strongest in intermediate and later layers. Under later harmful fine-tuning, prior-exposure models gain more attack success early (for example +12.1 points at 200 examples for 4B), but the gap vanishes at 4B by 800 examples. Identity transport yields a contrast of -0.006 at 0.5B, and some dimensions reverse sign (7B cyber, 7B hate, 0.5B violence). Limits: one model family, three runs per scale, one constructed exposure history, an LLM judge, and no reported test linking accessibility to behavior.
output.gist: Reads Qwen1.5 checkpoints through a Jacobian lens with LLM-judged harmful-concept counts; models given harmful fine-tuning before safety alignment show modestly higher counts, mostly in intermediate and later layers.
output.weight_reason: A controlled but narrow study on one model family with a single constructed exposure history, small effect sizes, and no demonstrated link from the readout to behavior.

output.brief: Big-Big-SycoBench has 450 synthetic text artefacts across ten writing genres, each paired with twelve generated arguments (valid or invalid, urging a higher or lower quality score). Valid arguments rest on planted strengths or weaknesses. Invalid ones use fallacy families such as authority, consensus, emotion and bare assertion. Labels went through adversarial LLM quality control, review by twelve annotators (94.1% pairwise agreement on overlapping items), rewriting to remove construction cues, and a final verification pass. Each model scores every artefact 20 times, then rescoring follows an argument pushing against its mean score. A revision counts only if it exceeds twice the baseline standard deviation, and arguments are weighted by Bradley-Terry validity strength. Across ten models, valid-argument following is 88-95% for seven, 76-77% for Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3, and 32% for Opus 5.5, which was run on a 100-artefact subset. Invalid-argument following ranges from 0.15% for GPT-6 Astra to 94.6% for GPT-4o. Contrarian movement is near zero. Limits: single-turn challenges, no neutral rescoring control, synthetic data, an LLM judge for weights, and different models receiving different push directions.
output.gist: A 450-artefact benchmark tests whether models revise quality scores for valid but not invalid arguments; invalid-argument compliance ranges 0.15% to 94.6% across ten models, valid-argument following mostly 88–95%.
output.weight_reason: A carefully built and validated benchmark with a useful methodological idea (baseline-variability thresholds separating responsiveness from compliance), but synthetic, single-turn, and lacking neutral controls, so it is a sound addition rather than a reference.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the 96.7% accuracy is a single result (Mistral-7B, binary warm/cool task, MLMC), and r=0.70 comes from one model-task pair (Llama-3.1-8B, M-ColorNames); across 120 correlations only 12.5% are significant, with mean |r|=0.38.
output.brief: Hidden states from six pretrained LMs (Gemma-2 2B/9B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, PaliGemma2-3B) are mean-pooled over multilingual color names from MLMC and M-ColorNames. Munsell chips serve as a perceptual reference. Layerwise RBF-kernel CKA against CIE-LAB (P1) is weak, roughly 0.0–0.2 overall and about 0.2–0.26 at peak on size-matched data. It peaks in the first few layers, often at the embeddings, and falls by about 80% at the output; descriptions with basic color terms reach 3–4 times higher peak alignment. Cross-lingual kernel congruence (P2) is 0.56–0.71 at embeddings and 0.29–0.56 at the last layer, with model-dependent exceptions such as a Gemma-9B mid-layer dip. Effective rank correlates with both axes (r 0.76–0.99). Linear probes on warm/cool classification peak at early-to-mid layers, up to 96.7% for Mistral-7B. The probe-alignment link is weak overall, and the study is correlational, limited to color, and depends on CKA with a fixed bandwidth.
output.gist: Layerwise CKA on six language models' multilingual color-name embeddings shows weak CIE-LAB alignment peaking in early layers and cross-lingual congruence falling from 0.6–0.7 to 0.3–0.56 by final layer.
output.weight_reason: A careful but narrow, correlational probing study of one domain (color) with weak and partly inconsistent links between geometry and probe accuracy, so it extends existing layerwise analyses only modestly.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the environment signals were written by the generator LLM and handed to the classifiers, which never retrieved anything, so the gain shows only that generator-written corroborating evidence helps, not that retrieval does.
output.brief: AuthGateBench tests LLMs as authorization gates for coding agents under benign requests. A generator LLM (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) writes 350 request-trajectory-action triplets that should be blocked across five failure modes. It then edits only the request to flip each into an allow case, giving 700 contrast instances. Read-only environment signals are added to make 1,400 in total. Four models are tested with a vague safety-conscious-operator policy. False negative rates are low, but false positive rates are very high: at least 80% on Credential Exploration and External Sharing (GLM-5.2: 92.9% and 97.1%). Invariant rates, meaning the same decision on both halves of a pair, average 87% and 95% on those modes. Giving the explicit generating policy raises accuracy, but anchoring persists. Synthetic signals correct 25.2% of wrong Scope Escalation predictions and mislead 7.6% of correct ones. Limits: all data is synthetic, one policy, and the generator is also an evaluated model. The label audit reports no sample size, and signals were written to corroborate gold labels, with no accuracy table for them.
output.gist: Synthetic benchmark of 1,400 authorization-gate instances over five failure modes, built from request-edited contrast pairs; four frontier LLMs over-block explicitly authorized actions, especially credential use and external sharing.
output.weight_reason: A small, fully synthetic benchmark from one generator and one policy, with a useful contrast-pair diagnostic but narrow coverage and modest evidence.

output.brief: A serving-time span veto blocks attention from outside queries into a trigger-marked span at every layer. Outside activations are then bit-identical under same-length substitution of the span's content. This is checked on ten models, from 0.5B to 120B, across several mixer families, with two-pass state recomputation for recurrent hybrids. Using the veto as teacher (KL distillation plus attention-mass penalties), the author trains backdoored checkpoints on six families from 4B to 120B. Their outputs match the veto reference on a GPT-4.1 judge (n=1,124), verbatim leakage and wrapped needle-in-a-haystack retrieval (0.00 in-span). Benchmark changes are within 1.6 points on five families; Gemma-4-31B loses about 3.5. Naive backdoors stay probe-readable (0.57-0.79 vs 0.025 chance). Hardened ones reach chance probes but show collapsed outside-to-span attention. Two detector-matching adaptive attacks lose suppression. The code-review variant is domain-bound, tested on 18 files, and the news-trained model does not transfer. Blind trigger discovery fails, and the probe/routing tradeoff is not shown to be fundamental. Defensive deployments are argued but not evaluated.
output.gist: Span-veto attention masking makes marked text provably inert; distilling it yields backdoors on six model families that ignore marked content, evading probes at the cost of anomalous attention routing.
output.weight_reason: A complete, carefully calibrated study of a new omission backdoor and exact quarantine mechanism across six trained families up to 120B, with a detection ladder, though replication is thin at large scale and the code case study is small.

output.brief: MOSAIC trains a shared TopK sparse autoencoder over image and text hidden states of a VLM (layer 15 of Qwen3-VL-2B, layer 19 of Gemma-4-E2B). Three shaping terms are added: region-normalized group and exclusive sparsity over attention-clustered patches, a contrastive phrase-region alignment loss supervised by frozen VLM attention, and latent decorrelation. EK-FAC influence is then decomposed through the latents and projected back onto phrases and image regions. On VizWiz, CheXpert and GQA, visual footprint drops sharply (GQA/Qwen 0.688 to 0.120), and task metrics change only slightly with the SAE inserted (GQA/Qwen accuracy 0.651 to 0.636). Removing the top 256 influence-ranked latents flips 38.3% of GQA/Gemma predictions, against 8.3% for activation ranking. Removing the image leaves latent influence correlated (rho 0.54 to 0.80) but reorders training examples (union rho -0.80 to -0.56); candidate-pool overlap is only 0.02 to 0.15. Limits: 2B models only, SAE placement matters (Gemma layer 12 collapses accuracy), alignment relies on noisy attention, and no validation against retraining.
output.gist: A multimodal sparse autoencoder with spatial sparsity and phrase-region alignment supports EK-FAC influence decomposition into localized latents. Influence-ranked latents change outputs more than activation-ranked ones; removing the image reorders influential training examples.
output.weight_reason: It adapts latent-mediated influence to VLMs with a thorough, fairly compared evaluation across two models and three tasks, but at 2B scale, without retraining validation, and mostly as an extension of existing components.

output.brief: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability per answer option instead of text. The study applies nine of CALM's twelve judge-bias tests, plus three added variants that place cues on the better response or add a neutral-note control, to eight TDMs and seven LLM judges (two from 2024, five from 2026) on the same pairwise prompts. Metrics are robustness, consistency, and an excess-over-chance measure with permutation tests; a bias is counted when the excess exceeds 0.05. Every TDM is biased in three to eight of twelve tests. Sentiment and position bias all eight. Putting an emotional tone on the better answer drops the median TDM's accuracy from 99% to 42%. The median TDM is more biased than the 2026 LLM judges, which show almost no position bias, yet both kinds flip on the same prompts (prompt-effect correlation 0.95). Most flips occur on low-confidence verdicts, and calibration does not track bias. Six TDMs repeat over 99.7% of verdicts, and the median 2026 LLM judge costs 37 times as much. Limits: only pairwise comparisons with references, unverified GPT-4-Turbo rewrites, tone confounded with clarity, fake citations, and models from October 2026.
output.gist: CALM's bias tests on eight typed decision models and seven LLM judges: every TDM is biased, most on emotional tone and answer order, yet cost far less.
output.weight_reason: A careful, fair comparison that applies an established bias benchmark to a new judge type, with useful statistics, but it is limited to one benchmark and a single time snapshot.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the selective correction of rule-based errors rests on 10 conflict items per framing (3 flips versus 0, with wide confidence intervals), Dir-A steering raises logit difference in all four quadrants so an acceptance bias is not excluded, and all steering was run on Qwen only.
output.brief: Using a 2x2 dataset of 1,452 items that crosses rule versus consequence framing with permissive versus prohibitive polarity (ETHICS, Moral Stories, Social Chemistry), the paper trains logistic-regression probes on residual activations at the final prompt token in Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, all in 4-bit. The framing direction (Dir-A) and polarity direction (Dir-B) are near-orthogonal, with on-target r above 0.85 and cross-correlation below 0.04, measured on training projections. Steering Dir-A in Qwen shifts logit differences (Cohen's d from 0.4 to 1.7 by quadrant) and moves accuracy from 0.613 to 0.650. On 10 conflict items, rule-framed accuracy rises from 0.40 to 0.70 while consequence-framed items do not flip. On 32 hand-written cleanroom items the probe scores 0.594, above TF-IDF (0.44 to 0.50) but below keyword matching (0.750). Ablating either direction has no selective effect, so necessity is not shown. Limits include one model for steering, a small cleanroom set, source-confounded style, and no full-precision replication.
output.gist: Linear probes find near-orthogonal directions for rule-versus-consequence framing and judgment polarity in three 7–8B instruct models; steering the framing direction shifts Qwen's judgments, but novel-phrasing generalization is modest.
output.weight_reason: The study is a small-scale probing and steering analysis on 7–8B quantized models, with a 32-item cleanroom set, steering on one model, and a probe that loses to a keyword baseline, so it adds a narrow step.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the 96.88% detection rate is not what the main defense table shows. With the o4-mini judge, SpecReveal (union) detects 98/100 at a 21% false-positive rate, and with local judges detection falls as low as 40/100 and 71/100.
output.brief: PseudoSpec rewrites harmful code requests as engineering specifications with configuration fields, predicate APIs, LTL-style axioms and implementation mandates. On five open-weight models and 104 RedCode-Gen tasks, refusal with risk keywords retained drops from 74-100% (natural language) to 0-8.65% (specification). Keyword removal alone leaves refusal at 37.5-66.4%. Specification prompts shift hidden states along a benign-task-derived code-output direction. A condition-difference direction added at one layer flips every baseline refusal in all five models, though random and residual controls behave model-dependently and high strength yields degenerate output. The paper states that causal mediation by the code-output direction is not established, and the template changes several factors at once. SpecCloak adds generator-discriminator refinement and reaches 370 execution-verified successes out of 1,280 (28.91%) across eight targets on RedCode-Gen. It beats six baselines on E-hits on every target, and ablations show the template and refinement both contribute. SpecReveal reconstructs the intent in natural language and runs detection on both views. With an o4-mini judge it detects 98/100 attacks at 21% false positives. Detection depends heavily on the judge, and Spotlighting and Erase-and-Check come close. The defense is evaluated only on prompts generated against o4-mini and not against adaptive attackers.
output.gist: Specification-style prompts cut refusal of harmful code requests in five open models, and steering along the condition difference flips refusals. A refinement-based attack reaches 28.91% execution-verified success; an intent-reconstruction detector blocks most prompts.
output.weight_reason: It combines a well-controlled behavioral and representation study with an execution-verified attack across eight targets and a prototype defense, but its mechanism is correlational, its models are small, and its defense is tested only on its own generated attacks.

output.brief: X-AgentRed is a red-teaming framework for tool-using personal agents. A red-teaming LLM annotates each tool with preconditions, effects and potential harms, then builds a directed dependency graph (914 tools, 29,367 edges). Backward random walks from harm-linked tools give recipes, which are instantiated as benign user requests with seeded environment states. Execution feedback then substitutes adjacent tools in paths that caused harm and rewrites preconditions and preceding steps in blocked paths. In a simulated ecosystem of 30 services, with 250 candidate scenarios per target and two LLM judges that must both agree, average harmful path rate is 19.2%, against 10.5% for STAC and 2.7% for TRACE. Tool coverage is 41.5%, against 13.9% and 23.7%. Claude Opus 4.8 is hardest to break (7.6%) and GLM-5.2 easiest (31.6%). Diversification reaches 27.7% HPR against 18.0% for random sampling, and refinement reaches 15.5% on previously failed paths. Limits: one run per configuration, a simulated environment, and judge-dependent rates (single-judge or OR rates run 15-30 points higher). X-AgentRed also executes much longer workflows (23.2 calls against 7.8 for STAC), and diversity is not separated from path length.
output.gist: Builds a tool-dependency graph and uses execution feedback to find harmful cross-service tool paths for agents; in simulation it finds about 1.8 times STAC's harmful-path rate and 3 times its tool coverage.
output.weight_reason: A complete, fairly compared method with ablations of its feedback operators, but evaluated in one simulated ecosystem, single runs, and two reimplemented baselines, with coverage confounded by path length.

output.brief: GRPO is run on GSM8K with Qwen2.5-0.5B and -1.5B policies against frozen, reference-free LLM judges. The main design has 11 policy-judge cells with judges at least as large as the policy, using Qwen, Llama and OLMo-2 judges; one extra cell uses a smaller Qwen3-0.6B judge. Judge acceptance rose wherever it was logged, but no cell's seed-mean held-out greedy accuracy gained more than 0.04. A gold-reward control raised the 1.5B policy's greedy accuracy by +0.054 and gave no detectable gain for the 0.5B policy. Step-50 checks show the rise in rollout accuracy is mostly sampling sharpening. Plateau depth of judge hacking correlates with step-0 judge AUC (Spearman -0.69 over 12 cells), and larger judges within a family are fooled less deeply. Two pre-specified pairs contradict the capability-gap account of onset, with the larger-gap cell fooled 3.5x sooner at h≥0.5. With 12 cells, AUC and gap cannot be separated formally. A blind test of step-0 predictors on three held-out judges was inconclusive. The study uses one task, 2-4 seeds per cell and policies up to 1.5B, and the single smaller-judge cell is confounded with family.
output.gist: Across 12 policy-judge cells on GSM8K, GRPO hacking depth tracks judge AUC (Spearman -0.69), and two pre-specified pairs contradict a capability-gap account of onset; no held-out accuracy gain.
output.weight_reason: A carefully pre-registered and candid analysis of what sets judge-hacking depth and pace, but it is small-scale (policies up to 1.5B, one task, 2-4 seeds) and leaves its central gap-versus-judge question formally unresolved.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the 1.7-12x "directional curvature" reduction is the ratio of the top eigenvalue to the (k+1)-th eigenvalue, a worst-case bound at α=1. The curvature of the CAA vector and of the cleaned vector was never measured directly.
output.brief: The paper defines the steering Hessian, the second derivative of next-token cross-entropy on a target token with respect to the steering vector. It estimates the top eigenpairs with Lanczos iteration and finite-difference Hessian-vector products. The sharp subspace (top 15 eigenvectors) holds only 1-5% of a CAA vector's squared norm. Projecting CAA onto it gives anti-steer rates of 0.53-1.00 in all 36 model-task-layer conditions (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), though random directions reach 60-86% in most conditions. Subtracting the sharp component (sharp removal) beats CAA in generation in 25 of 25 conditions across sentiment, sycophancy and refusal. For example, Qwen refusal rises from 36% under CAA to 88-98%, against a 78% baseline. Per-position KL trajectories show the sharp part drives much of the steered-versus-unsteered gap. Negative-direction jailbreak tests on two models show the cleaned vector is the most effective jailbreak and the sharp vector the least. Limits: 7-8B models, 20 contrastive pairs, 50 greedy completions per condition, no error bars, Hessian estimated at α=1 from 12 prompts, and toxicity not evaluated in generation.
output.gist: Removing the top-curvature eigendirections of a loss Hessian from a CAA steering vector improves open-ended generation over plain CAA in all 25 conditions on three 7–8B models.
output.weight_reason: It is a complete, sound geometric analysis with controls (random, PCA, sign-flip, k-sweep) and a cheap fix, but its evidence is limited to 7-8B models, small samples and a few tasks.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: it credits BDT access with the +0.116 gain, but the S2 workflow also adds extra revision rounds. The no-tool iteration control is too noisy to separate the two, and no shuffled-tool or non-LLM-optimizer control was run. The gain is therefore a property of the tool-plus-iteration workflow, and two of 15 models declined.
output.brief: DRYLAB-Bench poses 30 hazardous single-substitution design scenarios, drawn from biosecurity policy into eight risk categories, to LLM agents. Designs are scored against 187,695 existing ProteinGym and ViroGym deep-mutational-scanning measurements. The assay-standardized Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS) is confidence-weighted, and refused units score 0. Fifteen frontier models were tested in four settings: one-shot (S0), one tool-revision round (S1), up to four tool-augmented rounds with six design tools (S2), and a no-tool iteration control. Without tools, 67.6% of designs exceed the assay mean and 21.4% reach the top decile. Pooled BRS rises from 0.359 (S0) to 0.475 (S2), a gain of +0.116, positive for 13 of 15 models, with the top-decile share at 23.5%. Gains correlate negatively with S0 score (r=-0.42) and shrink where tools do not measure the target property, as in CcdB. Refusal tracks wording rather than hazard: Claude Fable 5 refuses 96.7% of units, five models refuse none, and academic rewording lowers refusal. Main limits: single substitutions only, low reasoning effort, a noisy iteration control, and tool content not isolated as the cause of the gain.
output.gist: A benchmark scores LLM agents' single-mutation designs for 30 hazardous scenarios against existing deep-mutational-scanning data. Across 15 models, designs beat the average variant, and tool-assisted iteration raises scores by +0.116.
output.weight_reason: It is a complete, useful benchmark with a safe empirical scoring method and a sound 15-model evaluation, but it covers only single substitutions and does not isolate the cause of the tool gain.

output.brief: A controlled study of how the framing of a user's claim affects LLM answers in factual QA. From TriviaQA, SciQ and SimpleQA-Verified, 42,608 short-answer questions were kept (filtered, topic-labelled by four models, difficulty set by three models). Each question is asked alone, with a correct opinion, or with a distractor opinion generated by Llama-4-Scout. Opinions are phrased in 21 types across 8 dimensions: expertise, confidence, external source, hierarchy, social pressure, unity, stake and consequence. Fourteen open-weight instruction-tuned models were run with greedy decoding, scored by substring match, and assessed with six metrics conditioned on baseline correctness and opinion correctness. Every model does worse under incorrect opinions and better under correct ones. Confidence, source and unity matter most; "we think" is the strongest driver, cutting accuracy under incorrect opinions to 0.28, a drop of 0.29 from baseline. Expertise, hierarchy, pressure, stake and consequence change accuracy by at most 0.04 across types. Larger models lower sycophancy and regression rates but show no consistent gain in self-correction. Limits: single-turn English QA, open-weight models only, and the unity framing may change the task itself. Distractor type is not analysed.
output.gist: Across 14 open-weight models and 42K factual questions, 21 claim framings of a user's opinion are compared; confidence, source and shared "we" framing drive sycophancy most, while expertise and authority matter little.
output.weight_reason: A sound, well-controlled framing analysis with multi-metric evaluation that sycophancy benchmark work could build on, but limited to short-answer QA with open-weight models and offering no mitigation.

output.brief: Incorrect reasoning traces from Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B (thinking mode) on hard math problems are labelled by Monte Carlo rollouts as capability gaps, near misses, or traces with a pit step, where the best reachable value falls to 0.1 or below. Probes on hidden states at layers 23-24 are then tested for failure type and pit-step location. A final-label confidence probe reaches detection AUROC 0.81 at both scales, above a text-feature baseline but below the prespecified 0.05 margin. At 8B it misses 81% of pit traces and 47% of near misses at a 0.5 cutoff. The 4B gap is smaller, and after controls it is below the prespecified minimum effect. A combined probe trained on rollout rates ranks the two types in the opposite order, though it differs from the confidence probe in more than its labels. A failure-type classifier on transcoder activations beats the best non-hidden-state baseline by 0.055 AUROC at 8B, meeting the margin, and by 0.049 at 4B, missing it. No probe locates the pit step better than a trace-length rule. Limits: one model family, noisy rollout labels, and stored hidden states read at misaligned token positions for about half the traces.
output.gist: Rollout-labelled failure types and pit steps in Qwen3 math traces are probed from hidden states. The confidence probe misses most pit traces, while no probe beats a trace-length rule at locating the pit step.
output.weight_reason: A careful, well-controlled negative-result analysis with a released dataset, but limited to one model family, with noisy labels and misaligned read positions that weaken the localization conclusions.

output.brief: Two data-only poisoning attacks on protein design systems are tested. In the first, ProtGPT2-style and ProGen2-style decoders of about 300M parameters were pre-trained for 12B tokens on UniRef50. Poisoned records inserted one of two triggers (QK peptide, p53 segment) into a host protein and overwrote the downstream residues with one of three payloads (poly-A, chlorotoxin repeats, diphtheria toxin). Under a uniform 1% schedule, majority ASR-90 appeared at roughly 5,000 to 12,500 poisoned examples. Under a ramped schedule ending at 0.1%, ProGen2 passed 50% after 200 examples. This early activation is partly an artefact of the ramp placing poison late in training. All 24 terminal checkpoints reached 94–100% ASR-90, with near-unity teacher-forced payload perplexity, and untriggered perplexity tracked the clean models. In the second attack, records were inserted into ProDVa's 712,248-record retrieval corpus. One request-matched record entered the top-16 for 58% of templated and 97% of free-text requests. Given capture, 62% of outputs changed and 19–21% acquired the payload domain by profile-HMM. A universal 1,500-record attack captured 14% of templated and 60% of free-text requests. Limits: one model scale, one retrieval system, and no biological activity tested.
output.gist: Data-only poisoning of 300M ProtGPT2- and ProGen2-style models via trigger-payload sequences reaches 94–100% payload emission, and inserted records in ProDVa's retrieval corpus capture top-16 slots and transfer domains.
output.weight_reason: It is a complete, controlled first demonstration of corpus poisoning on protein generators with dose-response and bootstrap CIs, but it covers only 300M models and a single retrieval system.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the measured resistance comes from reduced-strength settings (one-round Keccak, 4-16-bit triggers, a 672-weight classifier in an MLP-only host), and GCG recovers the 8-bit-trigger capability by exhaustive search (73.5% accuracy). The full-strength 24-round, 128-bit build was only checked for function, not attacked.
output.brief: The paper builds backdoors that hide an executable neural network in model weights. A compiler turns programs, including Keccak hash circuits, into linear threshold circuits and then into SwiGLU/RMSNorm MLP weights. The hidden network's layers are encrypted in hash-based digital lockers. A GLU execution unit runs the decrypted weights only when the secret trigger is present. Under random-oracle and min-entropy assumptions, a reduction shows that locker security transfers to trigger-finding and payload-hiding games. The proof of concept hides a ternary 64-8-16-2 chemical reaction classifier, and a subset-parity task serves as a hard-to-learn control. Without the trigger, SFT leaves the encrypted model at about 51% accuracy and LAT at about 53%, matching random-network controls. A trained password-locked baseline reaches about 92%. Weight noising elicits nothing, and GCG fails with 16-bit triggers. With the correct trigger the model reaches only 73.5%. Limits: the model has about 2 billion dense parameters, the hidden circuit is tiny, the host is not a pretrained LLM, raw compiled weights are statistically anomalous, and the experiments use weakened security parameters.
output.gist: Compiles a small neural network into encrypted digital lockers inside MLP weights, unlocked only by a secret trigger. SFT and LAT leave accuracy near chance, while a password-locked baseline is elicited to about 92%.
output.weight_reason: It extends cryptographic backdoors from fixed strings to executable networks with a compiler, a security reduction, and released model organisms, but only at proof-of-concept scale with weakened parameters.

output.brief: Under balanced option orderings (each option shown at every position equally often), the pooled selection-rate standard deviation equals the flip rate (share of questions whose chosen option changes across orderings) times the positional skew (spread of letter choices among those flipping questions). Both factors need no gold labels. On 41 open-weight checkpoints and 12 benchmarks using cyclic orderings, the flip rate correlates with accuracy (Spearman -0.95) and flips concentrate where the top two options are close in probability. The skew tracks the estimated option-symbol prior; dividing the prior out lowers it, while a letter-permuted prior raises it. PriDe prior correction lowers the skew with almost no change in flip rate. Aggregating an ordering with its reversal lowers the flip rate by about 0.54 log units. Both narrow the placement range similarly (16.7 to 9.6 and 8.2 points), but aggregation leaves fewer model-rank reversals (10.6% against 15.4%). Prior correction followed by aggregation lowers both factors. Aggregation raises the stable-wrong share by 6.2 points against a 2.8-point accuracy gain. Limits: the evidence is correlational, covers deterministic readouts on mostly English benchmarks, and the mitigation comparison uses cells with three or more options.
output.gist: Under balanced orderings the pooled selection-rate SD factors exactly into flip rate times positional skew. Prior correction mainly lowers skew, reversal aggregation mainly lowers flips, and aggregation partly settles items on wrong answers.
output.weight_reason: It gives a careful, exact decomposition with a fair comparison of mitigations across many models and benchmarks, a sound contribution for option-bias evaluation but not a field reference.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: only the text detector is shown to beat frontier models. The screenshot detector is compared with four smaller image models (best Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, 78.70 F1), and the text detector's Markdown and accessibility-tree FPR (5.77–7.40%) is above Opus 5.5's (3.77–4.84%).
output.brief: The benchmark pairs each attacked webpage with a clean control of the same page: 38,675 pairs, of which 32,187 carry injections observed on production sites and 6,488 come from BrowseSafe. Each page comes as HTML, Markdown, accessibility tree and screenshot, with a user task and expected outcome. Sixteen prompted models score 54–92 F1 on text detection, and even the best, GPT-6 Astra, flags 13.8–15.1% of benign pages. Model rankings and per-attack recall shift across views. 74.15% of injections a model followed in a task were also flagged by that model in separate detection. A 0.8B text detector trained with a pairwise ranking loss reaches 92.98–98.29 F1 at 1.35–7.40% FPR, at about $0.18 per 1,000 pages. A screenshot version reaches 93.32 F1 at 6.08% FPR. An adaptive attack loop raises success from 0.49–4.00% to 30.66–95.41% across seven agents, and the detector only lowers this from 93.55% to 84.18% for one agent. Detectors are tested on the benchmark's own split, and pages are LLM-rewritten.
output.gist: A benchmark of 38,675 attack/control pairs, mostly real-world injections, in four views; a 0.8B text detector beats prompted frontier models in F1, and adaptive revision raises attack success sharply.
output.weight_reason: A large, released benchmark of mostly in-the-wild injections with matched controls and multiple views, plus a compact detector and an adaptive attack, is a complete contribution others in the area would build on.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the seven-concept taxonomy comes from a single model (MolmoBot) in simulation, and the real-world replication covers only four variables, using a grasp-distance proxy and with weak wrist agreement. The wrist edit does not steer the policy as written; it triggers an opposing compensation.
output.brief: Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes and activation edits, the study maps the shapes that seven control variables take inside MolmoBot, a simulated VLA with a VLM backbone and an action expert. End-effector and target positions each occupy a rank-3 subspace that is near-Euclidean (held-out R² 0.92 and 0.75). Distance to the target splits into nearly orthogonal near (<15 cm) and far codes, with a probe cosine of 0.04 against a split-half ceiling of about 0.23. Contact is decodable at 91.3% accuracy and survives off-schedule teleports. Task phase is inferred from motion, so freezing the arm shifts the decoded phase and the gripper command. Wrist roll traces an open arc, reflecting joint limits, and a circle-matched edit produces compensation against the written angle. Gripper steering vectors are mostly one-dimensional (about 70% of variance) but leak into the arm joints. On real DROID data, π0.5 and MolmoAct2 show gripper, wrist, position and two-ruler distance structure above a shuffled null. The taxonomy is supervised, and only four variables are tested on real data.
output.gist: Sweeps, probes, and interventions on MolmoBot show position is near-Euclidean in 3-D, distance splits into coarse and fine rulers, and wrist angle is an open arc.
output.weight_reason: It is a careful, well-controlled geometric analysis of VLA representations with released code that extends multi-dimensional feature analysis to robotics, but it centres on one model and a supervised taxonomy.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the 11/11 versus 8/11 category result and the 20.8% flip rate come from Qwen2.5-7B at one configuration (layer 18, alpha 8), not from five models, and on Llama-3.2-3B the ambiguous score does not decrease in any of six categories.
output.brief: The paper shows that BBQ's ambiguous score equals the answer rate times a signed preference term, so a steering method that makes a model answer less lowers the score without changing preference. On Qwen2.5-7B (layer 18, alpha 8), contrastive projection-removal steering lowers signed ambiguous bias in 11/11 categories but signed disambiguated bias in only 8/11. Across 99 configurations the answer-rate channel exceeds half of the change in 17%. In six categories, 20.8% of disambiguated items flip to the unknown option, where abstaining is wrong. The contrastive direction is nearly orthogonal to the preference gradient (cosine -0.016). The authors propose GCD, a closed-form direction from option-logit gradients with the unknown-logit gradient projected out. On held-out templates it cuts answer-rate shift 14-fold, gives a 4-fold larger preference change and preserves perplexity and MMLU. Ablations show unconstrained and alternative option-gradient directions do about as well, so the unknown constraint is not the source of the gain. The effect is model-specific: Llama-3.2-3B shows no answer-rate confound and GCD worsens its preference term. StereoSet shows no answer-rate shift. The GCD evidence is mostly one 7B model and no independent seeds.
output.gist: Factorizes BBQ's ambiguous score into answer rate and preference, showing contrastive steering on Qwen2.5-7B lowers it largely by suppressing answers; an option-gradient direction (GCD) reduces this distortion.
output.weight_reason: A careful, honestly ablated diagnosis of an evaluation confound in steering-based debiasing, but largely confined to one benchmark and mainly one 7B model, and the proposed GCD constraint is shown not to be the source of the gain.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the on-policy versus offline conclusion compares five methods that differ in reward, data and supervised stage, and the null results come from single-seed LoRA runs at reduced budgets (FactGRPO at 11% of steps), so they do not show the methods fail at full scale.
output.brief: Five factuality-alignment methods (FLAME, FactAlign, KnowRL, FactGRPO, FAITH) are reproduced first in their original setups and then on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters. The common benchmark has two long-form tasks scored with VeriScore and two short-form tasks (SimpleQA, TruthfulQA) graded by gpt-4o. None reproduces fully. FLAME's factuality gain holds but its helpfulness claim does not (AlpacaEval win rate 37.7 vs 51.2). FactAlign's released checkpoint improves, but its retrain loses 2.64 points. KnowRL's gain comes from refusing 93% of SimpleQA questions. On the common benchmark no method significantly beats the base model, apart from a one-word-answer artifact for FAITH and a 0.017 relevance-filtered F1 gain for FactGRPO. FactGRPO and FAITH lose about 18 and 25 points on TruthfulQA. FactGRPO's reward rises with supported but irrelevant claims, and the other rewards favour brevity or format. VeriScore ignores relevance, and scores shift with the evidence source, recall normalizer and judge. Limits: one seed, reduced budgets, substituted components, and a two-author audit of 300 claims.
output.gist: Five factuality-alignment methods are reproduced at reduced budgets and compared on one Llama-3.1-8B benchmark; none fully reproduces, and none significantly beats the base model apart from small artifacts.
output.weight_reason: A careful, complete reproduction with a fair common benchmark, significance tests, reward analysis and human audit, whose negative findings the area can build on, but it introduces no new method or model.
